title: E-commerce Storefront Experience
summary: A premium skincare storefront concept with a warm neutral palette, strong product hierarchy, mobile-first layouts, and a streamlined purchasing journey.
role: Design and front-end build — concept work, no client engagement.
audience: Shoppers comparing skincare routines on a phone, deciding between three or four products in a single session.
problem: Skincare stores often bury the product story under decoration. The concept set out to test whether a calmer hierarchy — one promise, one hero product family, one consistent purchase action — would make the range easier to buy from.

showcase.title: Homepage
showcase.description: Single promise above the fold, one hero family, and a direct route into the catalogue.

showcase.title: Product listing
showcase.description: Four-up desktop grid collapsing to two-up on mobile, with filters kept off the primary reading path.

showcase.title: Product detail page
showcase.description: Benefit-first copy order, size and routine context, then the purchase action repeated at the end.

showcase.title: Mobile storefront
showcase.description: Thumb-reachable actions, sticky purchase bar, and no hover-only information.

showcase.title: Conversion layout decisions
showcase.description: Consistent CTA placement, fewer competing buttons, and trust content placed next to the decision point.

sections.heading: Project overview
body: A demonstration storefront exploring how a luxury editorial layout can be applied to a practical e-commerce journey without losing clarity.
The concept covers the homepage, catalogue, product page, and mobile experience as one connected system.

sections.heading: The problem or business objective
body: Reduce the number of decisions a shopper has to make before reaching a product that suits them, and keep the purchase action obvious on every screen size.

sections.heading: Target audience
body: Mobile-first shoppers who scan quickly, compare benefits rather than specifications, and abandon layouts that feel crowded.

sections.heading: My role and responsibilities
body: Information architecture, visual system, component build, responsive implementation, and speed review — completed independently as concept work.

sections.heading: Tools and technologies used
body: WordPress with WooCommerce, Elementor for editable sections, CSS-level performance passes, and a token-based design system for spacing and colour.

sections.heading: Design and implementation decisions
body: Warm neutrals carry the interface while product photography holds the visual weight, so the store stays calm even with large imagery.
The grid collapses in two stages rather than three, keeping tap targets above 44px at every breakpoint.
Above-the-fold JavaScript was limited to navigation; the rest of the page loads as static content.

sections.heading: Final deliverable
body: A complete responsive storefront layout: homepage, listing, product detail, cart entry, and mobile states, documented as a reusable component set.

sections.heading: Lessons learned
body: Product hierarchy does more for conversion than decorative detail — the moment the second competing button was removed, the page became noticeably easier to read.
Editorial typography works in commerce only when the price and purchase action remain the loudest elements after the headline.

deliverable: Responsive WordPress/WooCommerce layout set with a documented component system and performance notes.
lessons: One purchase action per viewport beats several competing ones.
Warm neutral palettes need a single dark accent to keep hierarchy readable.
Mobile layouts should be designed first, then expanded — not compressed afterwards.

title: Modern Shopify Product Store
summary: A clean, modern Shopify store concept featuring premium product presentation, clear product benefits, and a simplified shopping experience.
role: Concept design and theme implementation — no client engagement.
audience: First-time visitors arriving from social or search who need to understand the product in seconds.
problem: Product pages carry too much generic content. The concept tests a benefits-first structure with a restrained variant and purchase block.

showcase.title: Homepage
showcase.description: Category-led entry with one featured collection and a clear seasonal focus.

showcase.title: Product detail page
showcase.description: Gallery, benefit list, variant swatches, price, and a single purchase action above the fold.

showcase.title: Collection layout
showcase.description: Four-up grid with quick-scan pricing and no dense filter panel on mobile.

showcase.title: Mobile experience
showcase.description: Full-width purchase action, collapsible details, and readable typography at 375px.

sections.heading: Project overview
body: A Shopify storefront concept designed to make product discovery and purchasing feel straightforward across devices.
Sections were built so a store owner could edit copy and imagery without touching layout code.

sections.heading: The problem or business objective
body: Help a shopper answer three questions quickly: what it is, why it matters, and how to buy it.

sections.heading: Target audience
body: Mobile visitors from paid social, comparing a small number of products with limited patience for scrolling.

sections.heading: My role and responsibilities
body: Store structure, theme section design, responsive implementation, and collection/product templates.

sections.heading: Tools and technologies used
body: Shopify theme sections and Liquid templates, responsive CSS, image sizing passes for storefront speed.

sections.heading: Design and implementation decisions
body: Variant selection uses colour swatches with text labels, so state is never communicated through colour alone.
The purchase action repeats after the details block for long pages, without ever appearing twice in one viewport.
Collection cards keep price and title at fixed positions so the grid stays scannable while images vary.

sections.heading: Final deliverable
body: Homepage, collection, product detail and cart templates with a documented section library for future merchandising.

sections.heading: Lessons learned
body: Shopify's section model rewards consistency: fixed content slots kept the design intact when copy length changed.

deliverable: Shopify section library plus homepage, collection and product templates with mobile states.
lessons: Fixed content slots protect a design when merchandising copy changes weekly.
Benefit bullets before specifications suit cold traffic far better than technical tables.

title: Meta Ads & Conversion Tracking System
summary: A demonstration of how an e-commerce brand could connect advertising campaigns, website events, Meta Pixel, and Facebook Conversion API.
role: Measurement architecture design and event implementation — demonstration only.
audience: Marketing teams who can see spend in Ads Manager but cannot confirm whether on-site events are complete or duplicated.
problem: Browser-only tracking loses events to blockers and privacy controls, and mismatched event IDs can double-count conversions.

showcase.title: Event tracking architecture
showcase.description: Which events fire, where they originate, and what data each one carries.

showcase.title: Browser and server event flow
showcase.description: Pixel events and Conversion API events sent in parallel with a shared event_id.

showcase.title: Deduplication concept
showcase.description: How matching event_id and event_name values collapse two records into one.

showcase.title: Event testing checklist
showcase.description: A repeatable pass covering every key event before a campaign spends budget.

showcase.title: Measurement dashboard mockup
showcase.description: An illustrative view of event health — clearly marked as demonstration data.

sections.heading: Project overview
body: A demonstration of a measurement setup for an e-commerce brand, showing how browser and server events are structured, matched, and validated.
All numbers, dashboards and event volumes in this project are simulated for illustration.

sections.heading: The problem or business objective
body: Advertising decisions rest on conversion data. If events are missing, late, or counted twice, the reporting used to steer budget becomes unreliable.

sections.heading: Target audience
body: Small and growing e-commerce teams running Meta campaigns who need trustworthy purchase and lead signals.

sections.heading: My role and responsibilities
body: Event mapping, Pixel and Conversion API configuration, deduplication rules, GA4 alignment, and validation testing.

sections.heading: Tools and technologies used
body: Meta Pixel, Facebook Conversion API, Events Manager Test Events, GA4, and server-side tag configuration.

sections.heading: Design and implementation decisions
body: Every key event is emitted from both browser and server with a shared event_id, so the platform can deduplicate instead of guessing.
Event parameters were standardised (content ids, value, currency) before any campaign work, because reporting cannot be repaired after the fact.
A written test checklist became part of the delivery so anyone can re-verify the setup after a site update.

sections.heading: Final deliverable
body: An event dictionary, implementation configuration, deduplication rules, validation checklist, and an illustrative measurement view.

sections.heading: Verified results
body: None. This is a technical demonstration with simulated data. No campaign performance, conversion lift, or revenue change is claimed.

sections.heading: Lessons learned
body: Most tracking problems are mapping problems: naming events consistently prevents far more issues than any debugging tool solves.

deliverable: Event dictionary, Pixel + Conversion API configuration, deduplication rules, and an event validation checklist.
lessons: Standardise event names and parameters before launching campaigns.
Always validate with Test Events after any checkout or theme change.
Better measurement supports better decisions — it does not guarantee advertising performance.

title: Full-Stack Business Dashboard
summary: A modern dashboard concept for managing products, orders, customers, or business operations.
role: Full-stack design and implementation — concept work.
audience: Operations staff who check the same five numbers every morning and need them to load quickly.
problem: Internal tools are often built feature-first, leaving common tasks buried. This concept puts daily metrics, tables and states on one predictable screen.

showcase.title: Dashboard interface
showcase.description: Key metrics, trend chart, and status distribution in a single scan line.

showcase.title: Data visualization
showcase.description: A two-series trend line and status bars with text labels, not colour-only meaning.

showcase.title: API integration
showcase.description: Typed data contracts between the interface and the data layer.

showcase.title: Loading, error, and empty states
showcase.description: Every list has a skeleton, an error recovery path, and an empty-state explanation.

showcase.title: Responsive navigation
showcase.description: Sidebar on desktop, labelled bottom navigation on small screens.

sections.heading: Project overview
body: A full-stack operations dashboard concept covering metrics, tables, and the states that usually get skipped in demos.

sections.heading: The problem or business objective
body: Give a team one reliable surface for daily decisions instead of a spreadsheet, a chat thread, and three admin panels.

sections.heading: Target audience
body: Internal operators and managers who are not technical but depend on accurate numbers.

sections.heading: My role and responsibilities
body: Data modelling, API design, component implementation, state handling, and responsive behaviour.

sections.heading: Tools and technologies used
body: Next.js App Router, TypeScript, React Server Components for read paths, typed API contracts, and Tailwind CSS for layout.

sections.heading: Design and implementation decisions
body: Read-heavy views render on the server so the first paint contains real content rather than a spinner.
Loading, error, and empty states are treated as first-class screens designed alongside the success state.
Charts always carry a text equivalent so the information is available without colour perception.

sections.heading: Final deliverable
body: Dashboard shell, metric views, table screens with pagination, and a documented set of loading, error, and empty states.

sections.heading: Lessons learned
body: Designing the empty state early usually changes the data model for the better.

deliverable: Responsive dashboard application shell with metrics, tables, and complete state handling.
lessons: Empty and error states deserve the same design attention as the happy path.
Typed contracts between UI and data prevent a whole class of runtime surprises.

title: Conversion-Focused Landing Page
summary: A high-quality landing page concept designed around a single offer, a clear call to action, mobile usability, and a coherent message hierarchy.
role: Design, build, and measurement wiring — concept work.
audience: Paid traffic visitors arriving with one question: is this for me, and what happens if I click?
problem: Landing pages fail when the message, the offer, and the action are not aligned to a single path.

showcase.title: Hero section
showcase.description: One promise, one supporting line, one primary action above the fold.

showcase.title: Benefits and features
showcase.description: Three benefit blocks that answer objections in the order shoppers raise them.

showcase.title: Offer presentation
showcase.description: Price, scope, and what is included stated plainly with no urgency tricks.

showcase.title: FAQs
showcase.description: Real objections answered in-page so fewer visitors leave to search elsewhere.

showcase.title: Conversion path
showcase.description: A single action repeated at the decision points, with a secondary contact option.

sections.heading: Project overview
body: A single-offer landing page structured around one message hierarchy and one repeated action.

sections.heading: The problem or business objective
body: Give paid traffic a page that answers the four buying questions in order, without competing navigation.

sections.heading: Target audience
body: Mobile visitors arriving from a single ad set, comparing a specific service rather than browsing a brand.

sections.heading: My role and responsibilities
body: Message hierarchy, page structure, front-end build, form integration, and conversion event tracking.

sections.heading: Tools and technologies used
body: Semantic HTML, Tailwind CSS, accessible form validation, and Meta/GA4 conversion events for the primary action.

sections.heading: Design and implementation decisions
body: The navigation is intentionally minimal so there is one obvious path forward.
FAQ content is rendered in the page, not in a modal, so it stays indexable and keyboard-friendly.
No countdown timers or fabricated scarcity — the offer speaks for itself.

sections.heading: Final deliverable
body: A responsive landing page with hero, benefits, offer, FAQ, and a validated contact form wired to conversion events.

sections.heading: Lessons learned
body: Removing two of the three original buttons changed the reading order of the entire page.

deliverable: Responsive single-offer landing page with validated form, tracking events, and page-level metadata.
lessons: One page, one offer, one action — anything more needs a stronger reason.
Honesty in the offer section outperforms manufactured urgency for trust.

title: Personal Brand Portfolio
summary: This immersive portfolio itself — environmental storytelling, responsive design, accessibility, and modern motion design.
role: Concept direction, design system, and full implementation.
audience: Prospective clients and collaborators judging craft, taste, and technical execution in the first minute.
problem: A portfolio must prove capability while staying fast, accessible, and easy to navigate — the interesting constraint is doing that with an immersive visual world.

showcase.title: Layered environment
showcase.description: Parallax depth built from original SVG scenes rather than heavy video.

showcase.title: Responsive design
showcase.description: Mobile-first layout with simplified cinematic effects on smaller devices.

showcase.title: Accessibility
showcase.description: Semantic landmarks, focus management, reduced-motion support, and AA contrast.

showcase.title: Motion design
showcase.description: One coherent animation language with restrained timing and easing.

sections.heading: Project overview
body: The site you are reading: a cinematic personal portfolio that keeps professional credibility ahead of spectacle.

sections.heading: The problem or business objective
body: Be memorable within seconds, then make services, proof, and contact routes effortless to reach.

sections.heading: Target audience
body: Businesses evaluating a developer for a website, storefront, advertising, or tracking work.

sections.heading: My role and responsibilities
body: Creative direction, design system, component architecture, animation, accessibility, performance, and SEO.

sections.heading: Tools and technologies used
body: Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Motion for React, Lucide icons, and original SVG artwork.

sections.heading: Design and implementation decisions
body: Server Components by default; animation and pointer behaviour isolated to client components.
Original SVG scenes instead of stock imagery — zero image payload, crisp at any size, and fully on-brand.
Motion respects prefers-reduced-motion everywhere, with static artwork as the fallback.

sections.heading: Final deliverable
body: A production portfolio with editorial design system, cinematic hero, work explorer, case studies, insights, and contact flow.

sections.heading: Lessons learned
body: Immersion comes from layering and timing, not from the quantity of effects.
Keeping the particle budget strict and pausing off-screen loops made the difference between feeling alive and feeling heavy.

deliverable: Complete responsive portfolio site with design system, motion language, and documentation.
lessons: Restraint is what separates cinematic from noisy.
Accessibility and ambition are not in conflict when motion is opt-out by system preference.
